messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol was a 21-year-old Latina animator who came to treatment after months of feeling as though her life had narrowed around a childhood memory she could not keep at a distance. She grew up in a home where her father’s violence toward her mother could erupt without warning, and she described one night in particular that still anchored everything else: the crash of a plate hitting the wall, her mother’s sharp gasp, the sound of something heavy being thrown across the room, and the smell of spilled beer and cigarette smoke hanging in the hallway while Marisol hid behind her bedroom door and listened. Even now, when she thought of that night, the memory arrived more as a scene than a recollection. It felt more vivid and real than ordinary moments in her present life, and sometimes the odor of beer or stale smoke seemed to come back so strongly that she could almost taste the panic in her mouth. Yet when the image started to sharpen, she found herself pushing it away before she could fully follow it through, as if stopping at the edge of it might keep it from swallowing her whole.

In the years since, certain reminders cut through her quickly. If someone threw an object across a room, even casually, her body reacted before her mind could catch up. Related photos — especially images of yelling couples, broken household items, or family pictures that carried a tense atmosphere — could pull her back into that same dread, and related sounds, particularly slamming, banging, or a man’s voice rising sharply in anger, made her feel flooded and exposed. Those moments sent her straight into coping rules she had built around herself: she stopped making any plans for the future because plans felt fragile, almost inviting disaster, and she began restricting her eating with unusual strictness because controlling food was one area where she believed she could still impose order. She also avoided anything that reminded her of the person who harmed her, steering clear of certain neighborhoods, television scenes, and even family gatherings where someone’s tone or posture resembled her father’s. It was not simply that those reminders upset her; in her mind, they seemed to prove how quickly life could turn dangerous, and her attempt to manage them only made the memory feel more available, more pressing, as if every effort to stay in control kept the past close.

Marisol had come to believe she could not deal with even the slightest upset. She read her own reactions as evidence of helplessness, certain that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. Her irritation and angry outbursts at work reflected that fear as much as any mood shift; when a coworker moved abruptly behind her or dropped a stack of reference sketches near her desk, she could snap before she had time to think, then feel ashamed afterward. As an animator, she spent long hours at a shared studio table, and the unpredictability of other people’s movement in that space kept her on edge. She watched doorways, monitored footsteps, and scanned the room constantly, her attention fixed on who might come up behind her or what might be thrown. That hypervigilance wore her down, and the more she remained on guard, the more easily she startled to movement nearby, as if every sudden gesture carried the possibility of harm. In that tense state, fragments of the old scene returned more often: the plate, the smell, the sound of things breaking. What she tried to keep out of mind came back with greater force the moment she was keyed up, and each return made her feel even less able to cope.

Over time, the way she tried to protect herself hardened into a loop. She had avoided future plans so thoroughly that she had turned down opportunities to take on larger projects, worried that committing to anything beyond the next few days would only set her up to lose control. She ate with such strictness that meals at the studio became another source of vigilance rather than comfort. And because she kept arranging her life around avoiding perpetrator cues, her world grew smaller and more dependent on scanning for danger, which only confirmed her sense that she was never truly safe. She also held tightly to the belief that the people responsible had faced no consequences, and that absence of accountability sat beside her fear like an open wound: if nothing had happened to him before, why would anything stop harm from finding her now? When she finally sought help, it was after a week in which an animator’s headphones were tossed onto the table with a sharp clack, a related sound and movement that left her shaking for hours and unable to finish her shift. She came in tired, guarded, and afraid that her life would keep shrinking unless she learned how to stop living as though danger were still waiting in the next room.
